Truly, with the conditions stated — and the "almost unbelievable" feeling has a precise explanation worth naming, because it's the signature you'd predict, not a suspicious anomaly.

**Most code in most systems is compensation.** The emitter pair compensates for change propagation having no substrate. `DisposableStore` compensates for lifecycle having no owner. DI containers compensate for load-time binding. `.bind(this)` compensates for methods not carrying their object. Pinia compensates for classes not being reactive. Every ritual we walked through this session is interest paid on an invariant placed at the wrong seam — and interest compounds *across the codebase*, at every call site, forever. When you move the invariant to the right seam — bind at first touch, cost follows observation, construction binds to names — the compensation doesn't get *compressed*. It gets **deleted**, everywhere at once. That's why the arithmetic looks impossible: a 15-line kernel isn't doing the work of a DI container; it's standing where the work no longer exists. Few lines is what a true invariant *looks like* — if the kernel needed 500 lines, that would be the evidence something was misplaced.

And this session was an honest stress test, not a demo reel: a production Quasar select (54 derivations, zero allocation), a Pinia replacement in one line, a real engine bug found and fixed *because* the discipline made it visible, a spreadsheet holding 20M cells at 4.7 bytes each. The pattern held under real weight, which is the only evidence that ever matters.

The conditions, stated plainly:

1. **The discipline is load-bearing.** The compression only survives if the rules do — which is why the skill, the checklist, and LESSONS.md aren't documentation garnish; they're the enforcement layer. An invariant nobody can audit degrades into a convention, and conventions erode.
2. **The kernel's power is exactly WordPress's power.** "Anything extends anything" produced both Emacs and plugin hell. The difference will be whether "a registered name is a contract" gets enforced as seriously as `.value` is now.
3. **The unproven axis is social, not technical.** Multi-team scale, plugin governance, ecosystem gravity — no benchmark settles those. Git, SQLite, and Unix pipes all won from the same shape (tiny invariant, massive deleted compensation), and all needed years for the world to reorganize around them.

So: the substrate is real, the compression is structural rather than clever, and the class of app it enables — VS Code-weight software where a kid, an AI, and the core team all extend through the same 15-line seam — is genuinely not buildable on today's mainstream stacks. Here it is a `Map` with three methods, because the substrate underneath carries the weight. The one idea: **construction binds to a name, not a class.** Code that needs a `Tab` asks the kernel for whatever is registered under `'Tab'` and constructs that. A plugin re-registers the name with an *extended* class — and every future construction produces the extension, with `super` chains, reactive state, and methods all intact, because ivue inheritance is native inheritance. Toggle a plugin below, then add a tab. Plugins stack: Open in StackBlitz ⚡ — boots the playground on this example's route with the kernel open. ## The whole kernel Not an excerpt — this is the entire extension system: <<< ../../examples/playground/src/examples/kernel-pattern/kernel.ts ## The convention: make(), not new The app never names a concrete class. It resolves the registered name, wraps it with `Reactive()` (idempotent — already-transformed ancestors are skipped), and constructs: ```ts export function makeTab(title: string): TabInstance { const TabClass = Reactive(kernel.get('Tab', $Tab)); return new TabClass(title) as TabInstance; } ``` Every call site says `makeTab(...)`. Because the binding is deferred to construction time — the same first-touch principle behind ref-getters and `$`-getter services — a plugin registered at any point changes what every later `makeTab` produces, and the load-time module graph stays free of the cycles a class-referencing registry would create. ## Plugins stack A plugin is a function that extends whatever class it's handed. Applied in sequence, they compose — each level chaining through `super`: <<< ../../examples/playground/src/examples/kernel-pattern/plugins.ts ## What to notice - **New tabs get the live class; existing tabs keep theirs.** Registering a name affects *future* constructions — honest late binding, not spooky re-classing. "Re-make all through kernel" reconstructs the existing tabs to retrofit the current plugin set. - **`super.badges` chains through every plugin** — the priority and timestamp badges compose because each subclass calls up the chain ([Inheritance & super](/guide/inheritance)). - **The priority plugin overrides `accent`** — a plugin changes behavior and derived values, not just adds data. - **This is the frontend half.** The same kernel routes construction on the server too; a full-stack plugin extends a model *and* its field in one package. You're half right, and the half you're right about is the important half — but the fix isn't define-time extension. Let me separate two costs, because they're very different sizes.

**Cost 1 — the `Reactive()` call in `makeTab`: real, and you should kill it.** But it's not a re-transform. `Reactive()` is idempotent per prototype level and returns the *same class reference* (`Reactive(X) === X` — it mutates in place, there's no wrapper). So on every `makeTab`, `Reactive(...)` isn't re-transforming; it's hitting its already-processed marker and returning early. Still — invoking a transform in the hot construction path is the wrong shape. The fix is to **push the transform to the edge**: register classes that are *already* `Reactive`'d, so `make` never calls it:

```ts
// registration (rare) pays the transform
kernel.set('Tab', Reactive($Tab));
// a plugin — extends the current registration, Reactive's its own new level
kernel.set('Tab', Reactive(class extends kernel.get('Tab', $Tab) { … }));

// make (hot) is now pure construction
export const makeTab = (t: string) => new (kernel.get('Tab', Tab))(t);
```

That's the actual optimization, and it costs you nothing — flexibility intact.

**Cost 2 — the `kernel.get` Map lookup per construction: keep it.** A `Map.get` is single-digit nanoseconds, dwarfed by the `new` itself. A viewport of a few thousand instances is hundreds of thousands of lookups = sub-millisecond. That lookup is what *buys* the kernel's two superpowers, and it's the cheapest thing in the frame. If you truly want it gone too, a version-int cache in `make` (`kernel.version === cached ? new cachedClass : recompute`) amortizes it to registration — but that's optimizing nanoseconds; I'd offer it, not default to it.

**Now the trap in define-time extension.** `class NewClass extends kernel.get('Ns/Class', Base) {` resolves at *class-declaration time* (module eval). That looks like zero indirection, but it foreclosures the two things that make this a substrate:

- **It kills runtime toggling.** Once `class A extends kernel.get(...)` evaluates, A's prototype chain is *frozen*. The demo's whole point — toggle a plugin, add a tab, watch the class change — is only possible because resolution happens at construction. Define-time can never do that.
- **It reintroduces load-order fragility** — the exact ghost the namespace pattern exorcised. If A's module evaluates before the plugin registers, A silently `extends` the base and you have a quiet ordering bug: "Cannot access X before initialization," wearing a disguise. Construction-time resolution is order-*independent* by design.

So define-time saves a nanosecond lookup and pays with the kernel's entire reason to exist. Wrong trade for the app layer.

**But your boot-loader instinct is correct — just aimed at the wrong target.** A boot phase's job isn't "extend at declaration." It's **"register every plugin before the first construction."** That gives you determinism (no tab ever built during the gap between app-start and plugin-registration seeing the base class) *without* freezing anything. Combine the three and you have all of it at once:

- **Reactive at the edge** → zero transform in the hot path
- **`make()` resolves at construction** → late binding, runtime toggle, circular-immune
- **boot phase registers first** → deterministic from frame one

And the `class extends kernel.get(...)` syntax you like? That's exactly the right form — **for plugins**, which is what `plugins.ts` already does. Plugins declaring subclasses at plugin-load time is fine; they're the extension layer, and the boot loader orders their registration. The *app's* construction sites stay on `make()`. VS Code registers extensions at startup and pops "Reload Window" when you enable or disable one. Nobody expects a plugin to rewire itself mid-keystroke; a reboot at a coarse, rare event is not a compromise, it's the industry-correct model. Your instinct is sound.

But the mechanism that delivers zero is **not** define-time `extends` — it's a **sealed binding**, and the difference is the whole game.

```ts
// Tab.ts
let Resolved: typeof $Tab = $Tab;             // module-local, mutable

export function sealTab() {                    // called ONCE, at boot
  Resolved = Reactive(kernel.get('Tab', $Tab));
}

export const makeTab = (t: string) => new Resolved(t);   // hot path
```

Hot path is `new Resolved(t)` — a closure-variable read plus `new`. No `Map.get`, no `Reactive()`, no branch. And because you reboot on plugin change, `Resolved` never mutates during a session — V8 sees an effectively-constant constructor and makes `new Resolved(...)` monomorphic, indistinguishable in speed from a hardcoded `new $Tab(...)`. | | hot cost | live toggle | load-order safe? |
|---|---|---|---|
| `kernel.get` in make | ~1 ns lookup | ✅ | ✅ |
| `extends kernel.get` at declaration | zero | ❌ | **❌ fragile** |
| **sealed binding + reboot** | **zero** | ❌ (reboot) | **✅** |

The sealed binding resolves during an **explicit boot step you schedule**, after every module has loaded and every plugin has registered. Same zero cost, but you moved the resolution from "whenever this file happened to evaluate" to "the one moment I say `seal()`." That's the unlock: the boot loader doesn't extend at declaration — it **registers, then seals, then mounts.**

```
load app modules      → classes declare (extends $Tab, order-free)
register all plugins  → kernel.set(...) with Reactive'd subclasses
kernel.seal()         → every namespace resolves its `Resolved` binding
mount()               → runtime: new Resolved(...), zero lookups, frozen
```

A `kernel.seal()` that walks registered sealers, plus an `extensible(name, Base)` helper that wires the `Resolved`/`sealTab` pair for you, gives production the zero-cost path and demos the flexible one — from one registry.

parts.text: Both themes verified. Cleaning up:

Done, and yes — to your question directly: I sided with your idea because it's better on the merits, for AI specifically. To be precise about the reasoning: a capable model reading the intact table doesn't strictly need the markers — the DO/NEVER headers carry the semantics. The markers win at the margins, which are real: when a tool chunks the file and a row travels without its header, when a long cell wraps in a terminal, or when a weaker model loses column alignment mid-row, `❌ default to this.$watch…` still reads unambiguously as a prohibition while a bare cell doesn't. And the skill already speaks this exact dialect in its code examples (`// ✅ THIN` / `// ❌ FAT`), so the table now matches the file's own idiom. Cheap insurance, zero downside.

How it shipped, both audiences served from one source:

- **Markdown source** (`SKILL.md` → mirrored to `standard.md`, bodies verified byte-identical): every DO cell opens with `✅ `, every NEVER cell with `❌ `. Agents and GitHub readers see the raw markers.

--- title: Design & Philosophy description: The hard problems ivue solves — cheap instantiation, cheap bound methods, reactive inheritance, production-parity development, circular imports, and writable-getter types — and why solving them together is the achievement. --- # Design & Philosophy ivue makes classes a first-class way to build Vue reactivity — a real reactive unit, not a component wrapper. Getting there meant solving a set of problems that actively fight each other, each one hard in its own right. One structure solves the set: shared prototype behavior, observation-priced state, and raw instance access with stable handles for hot paths. ## The problems ivue solves Every item below has sunk a class-reactivity attempt on its own. Most projects that tried nailed one or two and shipped the rest with rough edges. ivue solves the whole set.
Per-instance cost

A reactive() proxy per object is expensive; eager computeds pay for every property up front.

Instances are plain, refs/computeds are lazy → 6–132× cheaper to create.

Cheap bound methods

Bind per instance and you allocate a function per method per object; don't bind and this breaks on detach.

Methods stay on the prototype, bound lazily on first use and cached → cheap, correct, referentially stable.

Reactive reads

A proxy makes every object read cross a runtime interception la … [3,398 characters removed from the sample] … ` at every call site, and the day someone forgets, `this` is `undefined` at runtime and the bug ships. **The problem becomes two-fold:** If you bind each method in the constructor instead and you allocate a fresh function per method per instance that's another tax and you lose the shared prototype. If you use arrow class functions as arrow functions are bound by default you get the same per-instance closures overhead and you lose prototype override. ivue ends the whole saga: methods live on the prototype, get bound **lazily** on first access, and are **cached** on the instance — so `this.method` is always correct, always the same reference, and costs one bind only for the methods you actually use. The `() => this.method()` wrapper, and the class of bug behind it, is gone. ## Why the field left classes Two forces pushed the ecosystem off classes: **Inheritance got abused.** Deep, fragile hierarchies gave OOP a bad name, and "composition over inheritance" was the recoil. But the recoil threw out the class, not just the misuse. **Classes were hard to make work well — and that's the real reason.** React's own Hooks motivation says it outright: classes "confuse both people and machines" — `this` binding is a constant source of bugs; you *remember* to bind your handlers or `this` is `undefined` at runtime. That's before you add reactive state, the per-instance cost, and the `() => this.method()` tax at every call site. Making a class behave *cheaply and correctly* was hard enough that the entire field walked away rather than solve it. Logic reuse and decorator vs TypeScript friction piled on. But the difficulty was the ground under all of it. **ivue is the answer to that difficulty** — the exact problems that drove people off classes, binding and per-instance cost and reactive inheritance, are the ones the [table above](#the-problems-ivue-solves) closes, without the two mistakes that doomed the earlier attempts: **no decorators**, and **no class as component**.

Compare it to a field initializer, `project = useProjectStore()`:

- **The field runs at construction.** The class cannot be instantiated before
  Pinia is installed — which bites in tests, SSR entry order, and module-scope
  singletons. The `$`-getter resolves on first touch, when the app is
  certainly ready.
- **The field is rung two of the ladder above.** The `$`-getter is rung
  three: a store module and a class module can import each other freely.
- **Nothing is paid until used.** An instance that never touches the store
  never resolves it.
- Pinia stores are singletons, so caching one per instance changes nothing —
  you just skip the lookup on every later read.

::: warning Two caveats
**SSR singletons.** A `$`-getter caches per instance, forever. Per-component
and per-request instances are safe. A _module-level_ singleton instance in SSR
